questions.topicName: Blood Pressure Control: Foundations and Frameworks
questions.stem: The illustration contrasts two segments of an arteriole: the one on the left has a markedly narrowed lumen while the one on the right has a widened lumen. What is the expected effect of the change shown on the LEFT segment on systemic vascular resistance and blood pressure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased systemic vascular resistance and increased blood pressure

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased systemic vascular resistance and decreased blood pressure

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased systemic vascular resistance and increased blood pressure

choices.label: D
choices.text: Decreased systemic vascular resistance and decreased blood pressure

choices.label: E
choices.text: No change in systemic vascular resistance or blood pressure

explanation.summary: Narrowing of the vessel lumen (vasoconstriction) raises the resistance to blood flow through the systemic vessels, increasing systemic vascular resistance (SVR). Because blood pressure is the product of cardiac output and SVR, a rise in SVR increases blood pressure. The dilated segment on the right does the opposite, lowering SVR and blood pressure.
explanation.whyCorrect: Narrowing of the vessel lumen (vasoconstriction) raises the resistance to blood flow through the systemic vessels, increasing systemic vascular resistance (SVR). questions.topicName: Blood Pressure Control: Foundations and Frameworks
questions.stem: This schematic shows a single hormone at the top branching into vasoconstriction, enhanced renal sodium/hydrogen exchange, aldosterone secretion, and release of a posterior-pituitary hormone that promotes water reabsorption. This coordinated, blood-pressure-raising response is characteristic of activation of which regulatory system?

choices.label: E
choices.text: The sympathetic nervous system acting alone

explanation.summary: The hormone shown branching to vasoconstriction, aldosterone secretion, ADH release, and renal sodium/water reabsorption is angiotensin II, the central effector of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. Its combined actions raise both systemic vascular resistance and blood volume, thereby increasing blood pressure. The natriuretic peptides and baroreceptor reflex oppose or acutely buffer pressure rather than producing this coordinated pressor response.
